en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 52.1 (SN 52.1, PTS SN v 294) 1. Rahogatavagga First Discourse on Being Secluded Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is secluded, he should reflect thus: ‘Is there any unwholesome state that has not yet arisen which, if it were to arise, would lead to my harm? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is no such unwholesome state,’ then he should dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute for the non-arising of that unarisen unwholesome state. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is such an unwholesome state,’ then he should make an effort to abandon that unwholesome state. Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is secluded, he should reflect thus: ‘Is there any wholesome state that has not yet arisen which, if it were to arise, would lead to my welfare? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is no such wholesome state,’ then he should dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute for the arising of that unarisen wholesome state. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is such a wholesome state,’ then he should make an effort to bring about the arising of that wholesome state. Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is secluded, he should reflect thus: ‘Is there any unwholesome state that has already arisen which, if it were not abandoned, would lead to my harm? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is no such unwholesome state,’ then he should dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute for the maintenance of that unarisen wholesome state, for its increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is such an unwholesome state,’ then he should make an effort to abandon that unwholesome state. Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is secluded, he should reflect thus: ‘Is there any wholesome state that has already arisen which, if it were to perish, would lead to my harm? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is no such wholesome state,’ then he should dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute for the maintenance of that unarisen wholesome state, for its increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There is such a wholesome state,’ then he should make an effort to maintain that wholesome state, for its increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reflects in this way while secluded, and he does not see any unwholesome state that has not yet arisen which, if it were to arise, would lead to his harm; and he does not see any wholesome state that has not yet arisen which, if it were to arise, would lead to his welfare; and he does not see any unwholesome state that has already arisen which, if it were not abandoned, would lead to his harm; and he does not see any wholesome state that has already arisen which, if it were to perish, would lead to his harm—then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very same seat, having attained final knowledge.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“For whoever has neglected the four foundations of mindfulness, they have neglected the noble path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering.
For whoever has undertaken the four foundations of mindfulness, they have undertaken the noble path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Venerable Anuruddha’s mind—just as...
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
even so did [the deity] appear before the Venerable Anuruddha.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“To what extent, friend Anuruddha, are the four foundations of mindfulness undertaken by a bhikkhu?
“In this case, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the nature of origination in the internal body;
he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in the internal body; he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in the internal body, ardent...”

Mindful and clearly comprehending, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, he dwells contemplating the nature of origination in the external body; he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in the external body;
he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells observing the nature of origination in the body internally and externally; he dwells observing the nature of vanishing in the body internally and externally;
he dwells observing the nature of both origination and vanishing in the body internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.
Possessing mindfulness, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
If he should wish: "May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive," he dwells there perceiving the repulsive;
if he should wish: "May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive," he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive.
If he wishes: “Avoiding both the non-repulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,” he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
He dwells contemplating the nature of origination in internal feelings; he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in internal feelings;
he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in internal feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating the nature of origination in external feelings; he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in external feelings;
he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in external feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating the nature of origination in feelings both internal and external; he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings both internal and external;

he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in feelings both internal and external—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Thus, if he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive;
if he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive;
if he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the non-repulsive and the repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive.
If he wishes: “Avoiding both the non-repulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,” he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Internally with regard to the mind... [and so on].

He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the external mind … he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in the internal-external mind … he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and vanishing in the internal-external mind, ardent … [and so on] … free from covetousness and dejection.
Thus, if he should wish: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive...
[and so on] ...he dwells there with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
[The same applies to] internal phenomena... [and so on].

He dwells contemplating the nature of origination in external phenomena … he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in internal and external phenomena … he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in internal and external phenomena.
He dwells ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
If he should wish: "May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive," he dwells there perceiving the repulsive...
[and so on] ...he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
"To this extent, friends, the four foundations of mindfulness have been undertaken by a bhikkhu.
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 52.2 (SN 52.2, PTS SN v 296)
1. The Chapter on Solitude.
The Second Discourse on Being in Solitude.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"For whoever has neglected the four foundations of mindfulness, they have neglected the Noble Path that leads rightly to the destruction of suffering;
for whoever has undertaken the four foundations of mindfulness, they have undertaken the Noble Path that leads rightly to the destruction of suffering."
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Venerable Anuruddha’s mind—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
appeared right before the Venerable Anuruddha. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...
He said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“To what extent, friend Anuruddha, are the four foundations of mindfulness undertaken by a bhikkhu?
“Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”
He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally ... pe ...
he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Internally in regard to the mind... [and so on].

He dwells contemplating the mind in the external mind ... [and] in the internal-external mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating phenomena internally ... [and so on].

He dwells contemplating phenomena in external phenomena... and in internal and external phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
To this extent, friends, a bhikkhu has undertaken the four foundations of mindfulness.”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 52.3 (SN 52.3, PTS SN v 297) 1.
The Chapter on Seclusion (Rahogatavagga)
The Sutanu Discourse.
On one occasion the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī on the bank of the Sutanu River.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Anuruddha; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Anuruddha.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Seated there, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Venerable Anuruddha, by having developed and cultivated what things has he attained great direct knowledge?
"Friends, it is by having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge."
Of which four?
Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in regard to feelings... [and so forth].
"I dwell contemplating mind in the mind... and phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—
it is through the development and cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness, friends, that I have attained great direct knowledge."
"And because, friends, these four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and cultivated by me,
I directly knew the inferior state as inferior, the middling state as middling,
and the sublime state as sublime."
The Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 52.4 (SN 52.4, PTS SN v 298) 1.
Rahogatavagga (The Chapter on Seclusion)
The First Kaṇḍakī Sutta.
On one occasion, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Sāriputta, and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were staying at Sāketa in the Kaṇḍakī Grove.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna emerged from seclusion.
Having emerged from meditation, they approached the Venerable Anuruddha. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Anuruddha.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Friend Anuruddha, what states should a monk in training enter and dwell in?"
“Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is a trainee should enter and dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness.
Which four?
Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is a trainee should enter and dwell in these four foundations of mindfulness.
The fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 52.5. (SN 52.5, PTS SN v 299)
1. The Chapter on Solitary Retreat.
The Second Discourse on the Thorn.
The setting was at Sāketa.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Friend Anuruddha, what states should a bhikkhu who is beyond training enter and dwell in?
"Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is beyond training should enter and dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness."
Which four?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; [he dwells] contemplating feelings as feelings... [and so on].

“He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—
friend Sāriputta, these four foundations of mindfulness should be entered upon and dwelt in by a bhikkhu who is beyond training.”
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 52.6 (SN 52.6, PTS SN v 299) 1.
Rahogatavagga (The Chapter on Solitude)
The Third Kaṇḍakī Sutta.
The setting was Sāketa.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Venerable Anuruddha, through the development and cultivation of what things has he attained great direct knowledge?
“Friends, it is through the development and cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge. Which four?”
"Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in regard to feelings...
in regard to the mind..."
“I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
It is, friends, through the development and cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge.
And it is, friends, through the development and cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness that I directly know a thousandfold world-system.”
The Sixth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 52.7 (SN 52.7, PTS SN v 300) 1.
Rahogatavagga (The Chapter on Solitary Retreat)
The Discourse on the Destruction of Craving.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, monks.
“Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Anuruddha.
The Venerable Anuruddha said this:
“Friends, these four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, lead to the destruction of craving.
What are the four?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body … [as in the full sutta] …”
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
"Friends, these four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, lead to the destruction of craving.
Thus it was said.
The seventh [sutta]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 52.8 (SN 52.8, PTS SN v 300).
1. The Chapter on Solitude:
The Discourse on the Pine-Hut.
At one time, the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the pine-hut.
There, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikkhus... [as before] ...and said this:
"Suppose, friends, the river Ganges were slanting, sloping, and inclining toward the east.
Then a great crowd of people might come along, carrying hoes and baskets:”
‘We shall make this river Ganges slope westward, incline westward, and trend westward.
What do you think, friends, would that great multitude of people be able to make the river Ganges slope westward, incline westward, and trend westward?
“Certainly not, friend.”
“And why is that? “Friend, the river Ganges slants, slopes, and inclines toward the east.
It is not easy to make it slant, slope, and incline toward the west.”
"And furthermore, that great crowd of people would only partake in exhaustion and distress.
"In the same way, friend, when a bhikkhu develops the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness,
kings or royal ministers, friends or colleagues, relatives or kinsmen..."
They might offer them enjoyments, saying:
"Come here, sir! Why do these saffron robes burn you?
Why do you wander about with a shaven head and a begging bowl?"
"Come, return to the lower life and enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds.

Now, friends, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who is developing the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness would renounce the training and return to the lower life. Why is that?

For it is impossible, friends, that this mind—which for a long time has been inclined toward seclusion, leaning toward seclusion, and tending toward seclusion—should turn back toward what is inferior. And how, friends, does a bhikkhu develop the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body … [as in the full sutta] … Thus, friends, a bhikkhu develops the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu develops the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu develops the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu develops the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu develops these things and cultivates them; and when he has developed and cultivated them, he is called a bhikkhu who is accomplished in view, accomplished in knowledge, an arahant with taints destroyed. This is the third simile for the bhikkhu who is like a thoroughbred horse. Just as, friends, a well-bred horse is called a thoroughbred because of his speed, so too, friends, a bhikkhu is called a thoroughbred because of his speed. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu swift? Here, friends, a bhikkhu quickly understands: ‘This is suffering’; he quickly understands: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he quickly understands: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he quickly understands: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is swift. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu powerful? Here, friends, a bhikkhu possesses powerful faith, powerful energy, powerful mindfulness, powerful concentration, and powerful wisdom. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is powerful. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu beautiful? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is beautiful, handsome, pleasing, graceful, possessing a lovely complexion, and endowed with a beautiful form. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is beautiful. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-born? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is well-born on both sides, of pure maternal and paternal descent seven generations back, unassailable and impeccable in respect of birth. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-born. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-trained? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is well-trained in the higher virtuous behavior, well-trained in the higher mind, and well-trained in the higher wisdom. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-trained. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-tamed? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is well-tamed, thoroughly tamed, completely tamed, and tamed in all respects. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-tamed. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-restrained? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is well-restrained by the restraint of the Patimokkha, well-restrained by the restraint of the senses, well-restrained by the restraint of mindfulness, and well-restrained by the restraint of wisdom. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-restrained. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-concentrated? Here, friends, a bhikkhu attains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-concentrated. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-liberated? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-liberated. And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-liberated in mind? Here, friends, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from the effluents, liberated from the fermentations, liberated from the obsessions, liberated from the underlying tendencies, liberated from the bonds, The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 52.9. (SN 52.9, PTS SN v 301)
1. The Chapter on Solitude:
The Discourse at Ambapālī’s Grove.
On one occasion, the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Grove.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion... [and] sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Friend Anuruddha, your faculties are serene; the color of your face is pure and bright.
By what dwelling does the Venerable Anuruddha now mostly dwell?"
“Friends, I now dwell frequently with my mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?
Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”
I dwell contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
"Friends, it is with a mind well-established in these four foundations of mindfulness that I now dwell frequently.
And, friends, that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal,
whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through right gnosis— he too has a mind well-established in these four foundations of mindfulness."
“He dwells abundantly [in this state].
“It is a gain for us, friend! It is a great fortune for us, friend!
That we have heard the lion’s roar from the venerable Anuruddha as he speaks in our very presence.”
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 52.10 (SN 52.10, PTS SN v 302) 1.
The Chapter on Seclusion (Rahogatavagga)
The Discourse on the Seriously Ill.
On one occasion the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Blind Men’s Grove, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Anuruddha; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Venerable Anuruddha, by dwelling in what kind of abiding do the arisen bodily painful feelings not take possession of your mind?
“Friends, for me who dwells with my mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, the arisen bodily painful feelings do not take possession of my mind.
Which four? [He continued:]”
"Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body as a body … [and so on] … feelings … [and so on] … the mind … [and so on]."
“I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Friend, while I dwell with my mind well-established in these four foundations of mindfulness, the bodily painful feelings that have arisen do not remain obsessing the mind.
The tenth.
The first chapter, the Section on Solitude.
Its summary verse:
Two [discourses] were spoken by him while in solitude.

Second Chapter: The Thousand Eons Discourse “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of a true man that lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time. What ten? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a true man is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first quality of a true man that leads to his welfare and happiness for a long time. (2) He is one who has learned much, one to whom the teachings have been well-mastered, retained, accumulated, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated by view. This is the second quality of a true man... (3) He is one who has gained a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade. This is the third quality of a true man... (4) He is one who has gained a good livelihood. This is the fourth quality of a true man... (5) He is one who has gained a good resort. This is the fifth quality of a true man... On one occasion the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Anuruddha; having approached, they sat down to one side together with the Venerable Anuruddha. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“By the development and cultivation of what things has the Venerable Anuruddha attained greatness of direct knowledge?”
“Friends, it is through having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge. Which four?
Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body in the body … [as above] …”
I dwell contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
"Friends, it is through having developed and cultivated these four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge.
And furthermore, friends, through having developed and cultivated these four foundations of mindfulness, I recollect a thousand eons.
Thus was the first [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 52.16 (SN 52.16, PTS SN v 304) 2. Second Chapter: The Taking Up of Kamma **Kammasamādāna Sutta: The Undertaking of Kamma** “Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of undertaking kamma. What four? There is a way of undertaking kamma that is dark with dark result; there is a way of undertaking kamma that is bright with bright result; there is a way of undertaking kamma that is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result; and there is a way of undertaking kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma. (1) “And what, bhikkhus, is the way of undertaking kamma that is dark with dark result? Here, someone undertakes kamma by means of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. This is called the way of undertaking kamma that is dark with dark result. (2) “And what is the way of undertaking kamma that is bright with bright result? Here, someone undertakes kamma by means of bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct. This is called the way of undertaking kamma that is bright with bright result. (3) “And what is the way of undertaking kamma that is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result? Here, someone undertakes kamma by means of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct on one occasion, and by means of bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct on another occasion. This is called the way of undertaking kamma that is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result. (4) “And what is the way of undertaking kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma? Here, someone is possessed of views that lead out, which are noble and lead to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called the way of undertaking kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma. These, bhikkhus, are the four ways of undertaking kamma.”

“Moreover, friends, it is because these four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and cultivated by me that I understand, as they really are, the result of the undertaking of kamma—past, future, and present—in terms of its basis and its cause.
The sixth.

Second Chapter: On Various Inclinations (Nānādhimuttivagga) Discourse on Various Inclinations (Nānādhimuttisutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these four inclinations. What four? The inclination toward sensual pleasures, the inclination toward form, the inclination toward the formless, and the inclination toward cessation. These, bhikkhus, are the four inclinations.”
“Moreover, friends, it is because I have developed and cultivated these four foundations of mindfulness that I understand, as it really is, the diversity of inclinations among beings.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 52.20 (SN 52.20, PTS SN v 305).

2. Second Chapter:
Discourse on the Destruction of the Taints “Furthermore, friends, it is through the development and cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness that the taints [are destroyed].”
“By means of eradication, having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
I dwell having attained them.
Thus ends the fourteenth [discourse].
The Second Chapter.
Its summary:
Mahābhiñña, Iddhi, Dibba.
The state of knowing the minds of others is a task;
the liberation through the all-pervading elements,
the faculties, the jhānas, and the three types of higher knowledge are [the fruits].
The Anuruddha Saṃyutta is the eighth.
